Notes: C#- C# Basics

C# Basics
​​​​​​​C# is an object-oriented programming language developed by Microsoft that is designed to be simple, modern, and powerful. It is used to build a variety of applications, including Windows desktop applications, Windows Store apps, Windows phone apps, and web applications.
Key features of C#
  • Object-oriented: C# is an object-oriented language, which means it is based on the concept of "objects" that represent real-world entities and the actions (methods) that can be performed on them.
  • Type-safe: C# is a type-safe language, which means that it checks the validity of data types at compile time. This helps to prevent common programming errors, such as trying to assign a string value to an integer variable.
  • Garbage collected: C# is a garbage-collected language, which means that it automatically manages the allocation and deallocation of memory. This helps to prevent memory leaks and other related problems.
  • Multithreaded: C# supports the creation of multithreaded programs, which can improve the performance of applications by allowing different tasks to be run concurrently.
  • Versatile: C# can be used to build a wide variety of applications, including console applications, Windows desktop applications, Windows Store apps, Windows phone apps, and web applications.
  • Interoperable: C# is interoperable with other languages, which means that it can seamlessly integrate with code written in other languages, such as C++ and Visual Basic.

Overall, C# is a powerful, modern, and easy-to-learn programming language that is well-suited for a wide range of development tasks.
Difference between Java and C#

C#Java
Operator OverloadingC# supports operator overloading for multiple operators.Java does not support operator overloading.
Runtime EnvironmentC# supports CLR(Common Language Runtime).Java supports JVM(Java Virtual Machine).
API ControlC# API are controlled by open source community.Java API are also controlled by open community process.
Public ClassesIn C#, there can be many public classes inside a source code.In Java there can be only one public class inside a source code otherwise there will be compilation error.
Checked ExceptionsC# does not supports for checked exception. In some cases checked exceptions are very useful for smooth execution of program.Java supports both checked and unchecked exceptions.
Platform DependencyC# is cross-platform and runs on both Windows & Unix based systems.Java is a robust and platform independent language. Platform independency of Java is through JVM.
PointersIn C# pointers can be used only in unsafe mode.Java does not supports anyway use of pointers.
Conditional CompilationC# supports for conditional compilation.Java does not supports for conditional compilation.
goto statementC# supports for goto statement.Java does not supports for goto statement. Use of goto statement will cause error in Java code.
Structure and UnionC# supports structures and unions.Java doesn’t support structures and unions.
Floating PointC# does not supports strictfp keyword that means it result of floating point numbers may not be guaranteed to be same across all platforms.Java supports strictfp keyword that means its result for floating point numbers will be same for various platform.

Keywords
​​​​​​​Keywords or Reserved words are the words in a language that are used for some internal process or represent some predefined actions. These words are therefore not allowed to use as variable names or objects.
There are total 78 keywords in C#.
Categories of C# Keywords
​​​​​​​​
Value Type Keywords:
There are 15 keywords in value types which are used to define various data types.

double    enum    float    int
long    sbyte    short    struct
unit    ulong    ushort    
Reference Type Keywords:
There are 6 keywords in reference types which are used to store references of the data or objects. The keywords in this category are: class, delegate, interface, object, string, void. 
Modifiers Keywords:
There are 17 keywords in modifiers which are used to modify the declarations of type member.

Method Parameters Keywords:
There are total 4 keywords which are used to change the behavior of the parameters that passed to a method. The keyword includes in this category are: params, in, ref, out.
Namespace Keywords:
There are total 3 keywords in this category which are used in namespaces. The keywords are: namespace, using, extern.
Operator Keywords:
There are total 8 keywords which are used for different purposes like creating objects, getting a size of object etc. The keywords are: as, is, new, sizeof, typeof, true, false, stackalloc.

Contextual keywords :
These are used to give a specific meaning in the program. Whenever a new keyword comes in C#, it is added to the contextual keywords, not in the keyword category. This helps to avoid the crashing of programs which are written in earlier versions.

Identifier
  1. Identifiers are the name given to entities such as variables, methods, classes, etc.
  2. They are tokens in a program which uniquely identify an element.
  3. Rules for Naming an Identifier:
    •   An identifier can not be a C# keyword.
    • An identifier must begin with a letter, an underscore or @ symbol. The remaining part of identifier can contain letters, digits and underscore symbol.
    • Whitespaces are not allowed. Neither it can have symbols other than letter, digits and underscore.
    • Identifiers are case-sensitive. So, getName, GetName and getname represents 3 different identifiers.
      Identifiers    Remarks
      number    Valid
      calculateMarks     Valid
      hello$  Invalid (Contains $)
      name1    Valid
      @if    Valid (Keyword with prefix @)
      if Invalid (C# Keyword)
      My name Invalid (Contains whitespace)
      _hello_hiValid
Variables
A variable is a name of memory location. It is used to store data. Its value can be changed and it can be reused many times.
It is a way to represent memory location through symbol so that it can be easily identified.
Syntax:
 type variable_name = value;
         Or
 type variable_names;
Example:
char ch = 'h'; // Declaring and Initializing character variable
int a, b, c; // Declaring variables a, b and c of int type
Characteristics of Variables:
  1. name : It must be a valid identifier. In above example, var is a valid identifier.
  2. type : It defines the types of information which is to be stored into the variable. In above example char is a type.
  3. value : It is the actual data which is to be stored in the variable. In above example ‘h’ is the value.

The followings are naming conventions for declaring variables in C#:
  1. Variable names can contain the letters ‘a-z’ or ’A-Z’ or digits 0-9 as well as the character ‘_’.
  2. Variable names must be unique.
  3. Variable names can contain letters, digits, and the underscore _ only.
  4. Variable names must start with a letter.
  5. Variable names are case-sensitive, num and Num are considered different names.
  6. Variable names cannot contain reserved keywords. Must prefix @ before keyword if want reserve keywords as identifiers.
Example :
int num;
float interest;
Initializing Variables
The term initializing means to assign some value to the variable.
Example :
int y = 7; // Declaring and initializing the variable at same time

int x; // Declaring variable x
x = 5; // initializing x with value 5

Data Types
  1. C# is a strongly-typed language. It means we must declare the type of a variable that indicates the kind of values it is going to store, such as integer, float, decimal, text, etc.
  2. C# mainly categorized data types in two types: Value types and Reference types.
  3. Value types include simple types (such as int, float, bool, and char), enum types, struct types, and Nullable value types. Reference types include class types, interface types, delegate types, and array types.
    ​​​​​​​
​
  • bool: Represents a boolean value (true or false).
  • byte: Represents an 8-bit unsigned integer.
  • char: Represents a Unicode character.
  • decimal: Represents a high-precision decimal value.
  • double: Represents a double-precision floating point value.
  • float: Represents a single-precision floating point value.
  • int: Represents a 32-bit signed integer.
  • long: Represents a 64-bit signed integer.
  • short: Represents a 16-bit signed integer.
  • string: Represents a string of Unicode characters.

int intVar = 100;
float floatVar = 10.2f;
char charVar = 'A';

String:
a string is a sequence of characters stored in a string object. Strings are immutable, which means that once you create a string, you cannot modify it. If you want to modify a string, you can create a new string that contains the modified version of the original string.
Here are a few examples of how to create and manipulate strings in C#:
// create a string literal
string s1 = "Hello, world!";
// create a string using the String constructor
string s2 = new String('a', 5);  // s2 is now "aaaaa"

// create a string using string interpolation
string s3 = $"The value of x is {x}";

// concatenate strings using the + operator
string s4 = s1 + " " + s2;  // s4 is now "Hello, world! aaaaa"

// get the length of a string
int length = s1.Length;  // length is 13

// get a character at a specific index in a string
char c = s1[0];  // c is 'H'

// get a sub-string of a string
string s5 = s1.Substring(7);  // s5 is "world!"
string s6 = s1.Substring(7, 5);  // s6 is "world"

// search for a character or sub-string in a string
int index = s1.IndexOf('w');  // index is 7
bool contains = s1.Contains("world");  // contains is true

// convert a string to uppercase or lowercase
string s7 = s1.ToUpper();  // s7 is "HELLO, WORLD!"
string s8 = s1.ToLower();  // s8 is "hello, world!"

Common string methods in C#:
  • string.Concat(string str1, string str2): Concatenates two strings into a single string.
  • string.Copy(string str): Copies the value of a string to a new string.
  • string.IsNullOrEmpty(string str): Determines whether a string is null or empty.
  • string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(string str): Determines whether a string is null, empty, or consists only of white space characters.
  • string.Join(string separator, string[] strArray): Concatenates the elements of a string array, using the specified separator between each element.
  • string.Replace(string oldValue, string newValue): Replaces all occurrences of a specified string with another string.
  • string.Split(char[] separator): Splits a string into an array of substrings based on the specified separator character.
  • string.Substring(int startIndex): Returns a new string that is a substring of this string, starting at the specified index.
  • string.ToLower(): Converts a string to lowercase.
  • string.ToUpper(): Converts a string to uppercase.
  • string.Trim(): Removes all leading and trailing white space characters from a string.
    using System;
    using System.Text;

    class Program
    {
        static void Main()
        {
            // Creating strings
            string greeting = "Hello, World!";
            string name = "John";
            string nullString = null;

            // String concatenation
            string fullName = name + " Doe";

            // String interpolation
            int age = 30;
            string message = $"Name: {name}, Age: {age}";

            // Length of string
            int length = greeting.Length;

            // Substring
            string sub = greeting.Substring(0, 5);

            // Index of substring
            int index = greeting.IndexOf("World");

            // Replace substring
            string newGreeting = greeting.Replace("World", "C#");

            // Split string
            string[] words = greeting.Split(' ');

            // Trim string
            string paddedString = "   Hello   ";
            string trimmedString = paddedString.Trim();

            // String comparison
            bool isEqual = greeting == "Hello, World!";
            bool isEqualIgnoreCase = greeting.Equals("hello, world!", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

            // Using StringBuilder
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            sb.Append("Hello");
            sb.Append(", ");
            sb.Append("C#");
            string result = sb.ToString();

            // Output results
            Console.WriteLine("Full Name: " + fullName);
            Console.WriteLine("Message: " + message);
            Console.WriteLine("Substring: " + sub);
            Console.WriteLine("Index: " + index);
            Console.WriteLine("New Greeting: " + newGreeting);
            Console.WriteLine("Trimmed String: " + trimmedString);
            Console.WriteLine("Comparison: " + isEqual);
            Console.WriteLine("Comparison Ignore Case: " + isEqualIgnoreCase);
            Console.WriteLine("StringBuilder Result: " + result);
        }
    }

Example: Implicit Conversion

float f = i;
Console.WriteLine(f); //output: 345

​
Conversions from int, uint, long, or ulong to float and from long or ulong to double may cause a loss of precision. No data type implicitly converted to the char type.

Example: Explicit Conversion
public static void Main()
{
    int i = 100;
    uint u = (uint) i;
    Console.Write(i);
}
In the above example, integer i is converted to uint explicitly by specifying uint in the brackets (uint). This will convert an integer to uint.

Difference between decimal and double
Both decimal and double are data types in C# that are used to store floating-point numbers. However, there are some key differences between them:
  • decimal is a 128-bit data type, whereas double is a 64-bit data type. This means that a decimal can store a larger range of values than a double, but it also requires more memory to store.
  • decimal is a precise data type, whereas double is an approximate data type. This means that when you use decimal, you can expect the results to be very accurate, whereas when you use double, you may experience some loss of precision, particularly when working with very small or very large numbers.
  • decimal is typically used for financial and monetary calculations, whereas double is more commonly used for scientific and engineering calculations. This is because decimal is more appropriate for cases where precision is of the utmost importance, such as when dealing with money.

Difference between StringBuilder and String in C#:
  • String: String in C# is immutable, meaning once created, its value cannot be changed. Any operation that seems to modify a string actually creates a new string in memory. This can be inefficient when performing a lot of string manipulation operations.
  • StringBuilder: StringBuilder, on the other hand, is mutable. It allows the modification of strings without creating a new string object each time. It's more efficient when you need to perform a lot of string manipulations because it changes the existing string instead of creating new ones. 
Operators
Operators allow us to perform different kinds of operations on operands. In C#, operators Can be categorized based upon their different functionality :

​

Bitwise Operators
In C#, there are 6 bitwise operators which work at bit level or used to perform bit by bit operations. Following are the bitwise operators :
  1. & (bitwise AND) Takes two numbers as operands and does AND on every bit of two numbers. The result of AND is 1 only if both bits are 1.
  2. | (bitwise OR) Takes two numbers as operands and does OR on every bit of two numbers. The result of OR is 1 any of the two bits is 1.
  3. ^ (bitwise XOR) Takes two numbers as operands and does XOR on every bit of two numbers. The result of XOR is 1 if the two bits are different.
  4.  << (left shift) Takes two numbers, left shifts the bits of the first operand, the second operand decides the number of places to shift.
  5.  >> (right shift) Takes two numbers, right shifts the bits of the first operand, the second operand decides the number of places to shift.

Conditional Operator
It is ternary operator which is a shorthand version of if-else statement. It has three operands and hence the name ternary. It will return one of two values depending on the value of a Boolean expression.
Syntax:
condition ? first_expression : second_expression;
Explanation:
condition: It must be evaluated to true or false.
If the condition is true
first_expression is evaluated and becomes the result.
If the condition is false,
second_expression is evaluated and becomes the result.

Example:
// C# program to demonstrate the working of Conditional Operator
using System;
namespace Conditional {
     
class Myclass{
     
    // Main Function
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
            int x = 5, y = 10, result;
             
            // To find which value is greater
            // Using Conditional Operator
            result = x > y ? x : y;
             
            // To display the result
            Console.WriteLine("Result: " + result);
             
            // To find which value is greater
            // Using Conditional Operator
            result = x < y ? x : y;
             
            // To display the result
            Console.WriteLine("Result: " + result);
    }
}
}		Output :
Result: 10
Result: 5

Parsing
​​​​​​​Parse() converts the string data type to another data type. 
For example, a parsing operation is used to convert a string to a floating-point number or to a date-and-time value. 

Syntax
To convert string into any data type, we use the following syntax:
data_type.Parse(string);

Example:
string var_string = "4.5";
Console.WriteLine(int.Parse("4") + 3);
Console.WriteLine(float.Parse(var_string) + 4.4f)
The int.Parse() method converts the string, "4“ into an integer value 4.
The float.Parse() method converts the string "4.5" into a float value 4.5

TryParse:
  1. TryParse is .NET C# method that allows you to try and parse a string into a specified type.
  2. It returns a boolean value indicating whether the conversion was successful or not.
  3. If conversion succeeded, the method will return true and the converted value will be assigned to the output parameter.
  4. If conversion failed, the return value will be false and the output parameter will not change value (default value).
    string input = "123";
    int number;
    bool success = int.TryParse(input, out number);

    if (success)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Conversion successful: {number}");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Conversion failed.");
    }
  5. Out parameter
    The out parameter is how the TryParse method passes the parsed value back to you.
    It's a parameter of type T, where T is the type that you are trying to parse the string into.
  6. Static method
    TryParse is a static method, so it can be called without creating an instance of the class.
  7. TryParse is used for many types like:
    intdecimalboolDateTime
    Enumstringbyteushort

​​​​​​​C# Input
Console.ReadLine(), Console. Read(), Console. ReadKey()

Difference between ReadLine(), Read() and ReadKey() method:
  • ReadLine():
    The ReadLine() method reads the next line of input from the standard input stream. It returns the same string.
  • Read():
    The Read() method reads the next character from the standard input stream. It returns the ascii value of the character.
  • ReadKey():
    ​​​​​​​The ReadKey() method obtains the next key pressed by user. This method is usually used to hold the screen until user press a key.

cmd line Parameter

To access the command line arguments in your C# program, you can use the 'args' parameter of the Main method.

Here's an example of how to access the command line arguments in a C# program:

static void Main(string[] args)
{
    // args is an array of strings containing the command line arguments
    foreach (string arg in args)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(arg);
    }
}

cmd line Parameter from Visual Studio.

To pass command line arguments to a C# program in Visual Studio, you can use the following steps:

  1. Open the properties for the project by right-clicking on the project in Solution Explorer and selecting "Properties".
  2. In the properties window, go to the "Debug" tab.
  3. In the "Command line arguments" textbox, enter the arguments you want to pass to the program.
  4. Press "F5" to run the program with the command line arguments.
Conditional Statements
​​​​​​​In C#, a conditional statement is a programming construct that allows you to execute a certain block of code if a boolean condition is true, and another block of code if the condition is false.
There are following types of conditional statements in C#:
  • if
  • if-else
  • if-else-if
  • Nested if
  • Switch
  • Nested switch
  • Ternary/Conditional operator
Syntax:

​

Switch case:
A switch statement in C# allows you to execute a block of code based on the value of an expression. It is often used as an alternative to a series of if-else statements, as it can make the code more readable and easier to maintain.

Syntax:
switch (expression)
{
    case value1:
        // code to execute if expression is equal to value1
        break;
    case value2:
        // code to execute if expression is equal to value2
        break;
    default:
        // code to execute if expression does not match any cases
        break;
}



Example:
int day = 3;

switch (day)
{
    case 1:
        Console.WriteLine("Monday");
        break;
    case 2:
        Console.WriteLine("Tuesday");
        break;
    case 3:
        Console.WriteLine("Wednesday");
        break;
    case 4:
        Console.WriteLine("Thursday");
        break;
    case 5:
        Console.WriteLine("Friday");
        break;
    case 6:
        Console.WriteLine("Saturday");
        break;
    case 7:
        Console.WriteLine("Sunday");
        break;
    default:
        Console.WriteLine("Invalid day");
        break;
}
// Output: Wednesday

Important points to remember about Switch case:
  1. In C#, duplicate case values are not allowed.
  2. The data type of the variable in the switch and value of a case must be of the same type.
  3. The value of a case must be a constant or a literal. Variables are not allowed.
  4. The break in switch statement is used to terminate the current sequence.
  5. The default statement is optional and it can be used anywhere inside the switch statement.
  6. Multiple default statements are not allowed.

Ternary Operator:

Iterative Statements
  1. C# iteration statement (loop) is a block of code that will repeat itself over and over again until a given condition is true or some terminating condition is reached.
  2.  The condition is anything that you want the program to evaluate before each and every time it loops. 
  3. Whenever the condition is true, the program knows to repeat. Once that condition is false, then it’s time to stop repeating.

arrays
What is Array?
Array are the homogeneous(similar) collection of data types. 
Array Size remains same once created. 

Simple Declaration format for creating an array 
type [ ] identifier = new type [integral value];

​

Advantages of Arrays:

  1. Random access to values stored at different memory locations.
  2. Easy data manipulation like Data sorting, Data traversing or other operations.
  3. Optimization of code.

Types Of Arrays In C#

  • Single Dimensional Array
  • Multi-Dimensional Array
  • Jagged Array

Array Declaration:
int[ ] integerArray; 
string[ ] stringArray;
bool[ ] booleanArray;
string[ ] student = new string[ 3 ];

Array Initialization:
string[ ] student = new string[ 3 ]{“stud1”, “stud2”, “stud3”};
string[ ] student = {“student1”, “student2”, “student3”};

Accessing Array Elements
Access Array Elements using Indexes
int[] evenNums = new int[5];
evenNums[0] = 2;
evenNums[1] = 4;
Console.WriteLine(evenNums[0]);  //prints 2
Console.WriteLine(evenNums[1]);  //prints 4

Accessing Array using for Loop
Use the length property of an array in conditional expression of the for loop.
int[] evenNums = { 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 };
 for(int i = 0; i < evenNums.Length; i++)      
     Console.WriteLine(evenNums[i]); 

Accessing Array using foreach Loop


int[] evenNums = { 2, 4, 6, 8, 10}; 
string[] cities = { "Mumbai", "London", "New York" };
 
foreach(var item in evenNums)    
    Console.WriteLine(item);  

 foreach(var city in cities)   
     Console.WriteLine(city);

Multidimentional Array:
2-D Array:
using System;

class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        // Creating a 2D array (3x3)
        int[,] matrix = new int[3, 3];

        // Initializing values in the 2D array
        matrix[0, 0] = 1;
        matrix[0, 1] = 2;
        matrix[0, 2] = 3;
        matrix[1, 0] = 4;
        matrix[1, 1] = 5;
        matrix[1, 2] = 6;
        matrix[2, 0] = 7;
        matrix[2, 1] = 8;
        matrix[2, 2] = 9;

        // Accessing and printing values from the 2D array
        Console.WriteLine("Values in the 2D array (3x3):");
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            {
                Console.Write(matrix[i, j] + " ");
            }
            Console.WriteLine();
        }
    }
}

3-D Array:
using System;

class Program
{
    static void Main()
    {
        // Creating a 3D array (2x3x4)
        int[,,] threeDArray = new int[2, 3, 4];

        // Initializing values in the 3D array
        for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            {
                for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++)
                {
                    threeDArray[i, j, k] = i + j + k;
                }
            }
        }

        // Accessing and printing values from the 3D array
        Console.WriteLine("Values in the 3D array (2x3x4):");
        for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++)
            {
                for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++)
                {
                    Console.Write(threeDArray[i, j, k] + " ");
                }
                Console.WriteLine();
            }
            Console.WriteLine();
        }
    }
}

​​​​​​​Jagged Array
  1. ​​​​​​​Jagged array is a array of arrays such that member arrays can be of different sizes. 
  2. In other words, the length of each array index can differ.
  3. The elements of Jagged Array are reference types and initialized to null by default. 
  4. Here, the number of rows will be fixed at the declaration time, but you can vary the number of columns.

Declaration
In Jagged arrays, user has to provide the number of rows only. If the user is also going to provide the number of columns, then this array will be no more Jagged Array.

Syntax:
data_type[][] name_of_array = new data_type[rows][] 

Example:
int[][] jagged_arr = new int[4][]
 a single-dimensional array is declared that has 4 elements(rows), each of which is a 1-D array of integers.

The elements of Jagged Array must be initialized before its use. You can separately initialize each array element. There are many ways to initialize the Jagged array’s element.

Initialization
Example 1:
jagged_arr[0] = new int[2];
jagged_arr[1] = new int[4];
jagged_arr[2] = new int[6];
jagged_arr[3] = new int[7];
The first row or element is an array of 2 integers.
The second row or element is an array of 4 integers.
The third row or element is an array of 6 integers.
The fourth row or element is an array of 7 integers.

Example 2: 
When the array size is not needed then its elements can be initialized with direct values as follows:
jagged_arr[0] = new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4};
jagged_arr[1] = new int[] {11, 34, 67};
jagged_arr[2] = new int[] {89, 23};
jagged_arr[3] = new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99};

Declaration as well as Initialization

Using the Direct Method
int[][] jagged_arr = new int[][] {   
 new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4},    
new int[] {11, 34, 67},   
 new int[] {89, 23},   
 new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99}};

Using Short-hand Method
int[][] jagged_arr = {    new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4},    
new int[] {11, 34, 67},    
new int[] {89, 23},   
 new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99}
};

Accessing the Elements

To access the elements of the Jagged array user has to specify the row and column with the array name.
Example:
// Accessing & Assigning 99 to the third element ([2]) of the second array ([1])
jagged_arr[1][2] = 99; 
// Accessing & Assigning 47 to the first element ([0]) of the fourth array ([3]):
jagged_arr[3][0] = 47;

Jagged Array
​​​​​​​Jagged array is a array of arrays such that member arrays can be of different sizes. 
In other words, the length of each array index can differ.
 The elements of Jagged Array are reference types and initialized to null by default. Jagged Array can also be mixed with multidimensional arrays. 
Here, the number of rows will be fixed at the declaration time, but you can vary the number of columns.
Declaration
In Jagged arrays, user has to provide the number of rows only. If the user is also going to provide the number of columns, then this array will be no more Jagged Array.

Syntax:
data_type[][] name_of_array = new data_type[rows][] 

Example:
int[][] jagged_arr = new int[4][]
 a single-dimensional array is declared that has 4 elements(rows), each of which is a 1-D array of integers.

The elements of Jagged Array must be initialized before its use. You can separately initialize each array element. There are many ways to initialize the Jagged array’s element.

Initialization
Example 1:
jagged_arr[0] = new int[2];
jagged_arr[1] = new int[4];
jagged_arr[2] = new int[6];
jagged_arr[3] = new int[7];

The first row or element is an array of 2 integers.
The second row or element is an array of 4 integers.
The third row or element is an array of 6 integers.
The fourth row or element is an array of 7 integers.

Example 2: When the array size is not needed then its elements can be initialized with direct values as follows:
jagged_arr[0] = new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4};
jagged_arr[1] = new int[] {11, 34, 67};
jagged_arr[2] = new int[] {89, 23};
jagged_arr[3] = new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99};

Declaration as well as Initialization

Using the Direct Method
int[][] jagged_arr = new int[][] {   
 new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4},    
new int[] {11, 34, 67},   
 new int[] {89, 23},   
 new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99}};
Using Short-hand Method
int[][] jagged_arr = {    new int[] {1, 2, 3, 4},    
new int[] {11, 34, 67},    
new int[] {89, 23},   
 new int[] {0, 45, 78, 53, 99}
};

Accessing the Elements

To access the elements of the Jagged array user has to specify the row and column with the array name.

Example:
// Accessing & Assigning 99 to the third element ([2]) of the second array ([1])
jagged_arr[1][2] = 99; 
// Accessing & Assigning 47 to the first element ([0]) of the fourth array ([3]):
jagged_arr[3][0] = 47;

Console Applications
Create the app
Create a .NET console app project named "HelloWorld".
  1. Start Visual Studio 2022.
  2. On the start page, choose Create a new project.
​

3. On the Create a new project page, enter console in the search box. Next, choose C# or Visual Basic from the language list, and then choose All platforms from the platform list. Choose the Console Application template, and then choose Next.

​

4. In the Configure your new project dialog, enter HelloWorld in the Project name box. Then choose Next.

​
Configure your new project window with Project name, location, and solution name fields

5. In the Additional information dialog:
  • Select .NET 6 (Long-term support).
  • Select Do not use top-level statements.
  • Select Create.
The template creates a simple application that displays "Hello World" in the console window. The code is in the Program.cs or Program.cs file:
​​​​​​​
namespace HelloWorld;
 internal class Program
 {
     static void Main(string[] args)
     {
         Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!");
     }
 }

Run the app
Press Ctrl+F5 to run the program without debugging.
A console window opens with the text "Hello World!" printed on the screen.
Console window showing Hello World Press any key to continue
Press any key to close the console window.
